subject: biology
title: The immune system
summary: How the body defends itself against pathogens: physical and chemical barriers, white blood cells, inflammation, and how antibodies and memory cells give long-lasting protection.
body:
Every day your body meets millions of microorganisms, yet you are only sick now and then. That is because of your **immune system**, the group of organs, cells and chemicals that protects the body from pathogens. It works in layers: first it tries to keep pathogens out, then it attacks any that get in, and finally it remembers them so it can respond faster next time.

## Key ideas

### Three lines of defence

A useful way to organise the immune system is into three lines of defence:

| Line of defence | What it does | Specific or non-specific? |
|---|---|---|
| First line | Barriers that stop pathogens entering | Non-specific |
| Second line | Cells and responses that attack any invader inside the body | Non-specific |
| Third line | Lymphocytes that target one particular pathogen and remember it | Specific |

A **non-specific** defence works the same way against any pathogen. A **specific** defence targets one particular pathogen.

### First line: barriers

**Physical barriers** block pathogens:

- **Skin**: a tough, waterproof outer layer of dead cells that most pathogens cannot get through unless it is cut.
- **Mucous membranes**: linings of the nose, throat and airways produce sticky **mucus** that traps pathogens.
- **Cilia**: tiny hair-like structures in the airways that beat to sweep mucus up and away from the lungs.

**Chemical barriers** kill or slow pathogens:

- **Stomach acid** kills many pathogens swallowed with food.
- Tears, saliva and sweat contain substances such as **lysozyme**, an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls.

Reflexes such as coughing and sneezing also help push pathogens out.

### Second line: white blood cells and inflammation

If a pathogen gets past the barriers, for example through a cut, the second line responds. **White blood cells** are cells in the blood and tissues that defend the body.

**Phagocytes** are white blood cells that engulf (swallow) pathogens and digest them. This process is called **phagocytosis**. The phagocyte wraps its membrane around the pathogen, encloses it in a sac and breaks it down with enzymes.

**Inflammation** is the body's response to injury or infection in a tissue. Damaged cells release chemical signals (such as **histamine**). These cause:

- Blood vessels nearby to widen, bringing more blood, which causes **redness** and **heat**.
- Vessel walls to become leakier, so fluid and white blood cells move into the tissue, causing **swelling**.
- **Pain**, as swelling and chemicals affect nerve endings.

Inflammation is helpful: it brings phagocytes to the site quickly. A **fever**, a rise in body temperature, can also help by slowing the growth of some pathogens and speeding up immune responses.

### Third line: antibodies and memory cells

The third line is the specific response, carried out by white blood cells called **lymphocytes**. There are two main kinds:

- **B cells**, which make antibodies.
- **T cells**, which help control the response and can destroy body cells that are infected (for example, by a virus).

Every pathogen has molecules on its surface that the immune system can recognise as foreign. These are called **antigens**. Each B cell can recognise one antigen shape only.

**Antibodies** are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells. Each antibody has a binding site that fits one specific antigen, like a lock and key. When antibodies attach to a pathogen, they:

- clump pathogens together so phagocytes can engulf them more easily
- block viruses from entering cells
- neutralise toxins
- mark pathogens for destruction.

When a B cell meets its matching antigen (usually with help from T cells), it divides many times. Most of the new cells become **plasma cells**, which release large numbers of antibodies. Some become **memory cells**, which stay in the body for a long time. If the same pathogen returns, memory cells recognise it and trigger a much faster and stronger response, often destroying it before you feel sick. This is called **immunity**.

### Why you catch colds again and again

Antibodies are specific. Immunity to one pathogen does not protect against a different one. There are many different viruses that cause colds, and some viruses (such as influenza) change their antigens over time, so memory cells may not recognise them.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Matching the defence

**Scenario:** For each event, name the line of defence.
(a) Mucus in the nose traps dust and bacteria.
(b) A phagocyte engulfs bacteria at a splinter wound.
(c) A person makes antibodies against the measles virus.

**Step 1:** (a) Mucus stops pathogens entering. This is a barrier, so it is the **first line**.
**Step 2:** (b) The phagocyte attacks any bacteria in the tissue, not one specific type. This is the **second line**.
**Step 3:** (c) The antibodies fit only measles antigens. This is specific, so it is the **third line**.

### Example 2: Reading a graph of antibody levels

**Scenario:** A graph shows a person's antibody level against a virus. After the first infection, antibodies take about a week to rise, reach a low peak, then fall. Months later the person meets the same virus again. This time antibodies rise within a couple of days and reach a much higher peak. Explain the difference.

**Step 1:** In the first infection, only a few B cells match the antigen. They take time to divide and make plasma cells, so the response is slow and small.
**Step 2:** That first response also made memory cells.
**Step 3:** In the second infection, the many memory cells recognise the antigen quickly and rapidly form plasma cells.

**Answer:** The second response is faster and larger because memory cells were made during the first infection.

## Common mistakes

- Saying antibodies "eat" pathogens. Phagocytes engulf pathogens; antibodies are proteins that bind to antigens.
- Mixing up antigens and antibodies. Antigens are on the pathogen; antibodies are made by your B cells.
- Thinking inflammation is always harmful. In the short term it helps fight infection.
- Thinking one antibody works against all pathogens. Each antibody fits one antigen shape.
- Calling skin and stomach acid "specific". All first-line barriers are non-specific.

## Exam tips

- Learn the three lines of defence with one example each, and whether each is specific or non-specific.
- When describing antibodies, use the word **specific** and mention that they bind to a matching antigen.
- In graph questions about a second infection, mention memory cells and say the response is faster and greater.
- VCE Biology Unit 3 builds on this in more detail, so get the basic terms right now.

## Tips to remember

- **Picture a castle:** the first line is the walls and moat (skin, mucus, stomach acid), the second line is the guards who attack anyone (phagocytes, inflammation), and the third line is the special forces trained for one enemy (B and T cells).
- **"AntiGEN GENerates antibodies."** Antigens are on the pathogen; antibodies are made by your B cells.
- **Antibodies are a lock and key.** Each Y-shaped antibody fits one antigen shape only.
- **"Phago" means "eat".** Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens. Antibodies don't eat anything; they bind and clump.
- **Signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain.** All four come from wider, leakier blood vessels bringing white blood cells to the site.
- **Memory cells are the immune system's "wanted poster".** They make the response faster and stronger the next time the same pathogen turns up.

## Key terms

- **Immune system** — the organs, cells and chemicals that defend the body against pathogens.
- **Non-specific defence** — a defence that works the same way against any pathogen.
- **Specific defence** — a defence that targets one particular pathogen.
- **Phagocyte** — a white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens.
- **Inflammation** — redness, heat, swelling and pain at a site of injury or infection, bringing white blood cells to it.
- **Lymphocyte** — a white blood cell (B or T cell) involved in the specific response.
- **Antigen** — a molecule on a pathogen that the immune system recognises as foreign.
- **Antibody** — a Y-shaped protein made by B cells that binds to a specific antigen.
- **Memory cell** — a long-lived lymphocyte that remembers an antigen.
- **Immunity** — the ability to resist a disease because of an earlier response.

## Summary

- The immune system has three lines of defence: barriers, non-specific responses and specific responses.
- Skin, mucus, cilia and chemicals such as stomach acid form the first line.
- Phagocytes and inflammation form the second line and act against any pathogen.
- B cells make antibodies that bind to specific antigens; T cells help and destroy infected cells.
- Memory cells give a faster, stronger response if the same pathogen returns, which is immunity.

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of the first line of defence?
questions.explanation: Stomach acid is a chemical barrier that kills pathogens before they enter body tissues. Phagocytes are tempting, but they act after a pathogen has got inside, so they are the second line.

options.A: Proteins made by B cells that bind to specific antigens
options.B: White blood cells that engulf pathogens
options.C: Molecules on the surface of pathogens
options.D: Chemicals that cause redness and swelling

questions.explanation: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells (plasma cells) that fit one antigen. Option C describes antigens, which are easy to confuse with antibodies.

questions.prompt: Why does a cut finger often become red and swollen?

options.A: Antibodies are clumping together under the skin
options.B: Blood vessels widen and leak, bringing fluid and white blood cells to the site
options.C: The skin is producing extra mucus
options.D: Memory cells are dividing in the wound

questions.explanation: During inflammation, chemical signals widen vessels (redness, heat) and make them leaky (swelling), so phagocytes reach the site. Clumping antibodies do not cause visible swelling.

questions.prompt: Why is the third line of defence described as specific?

options.A: It only works in specific organs
options.C: Each antibody and lymphocyte responds to one particular antigen
options.D: It is the first defence to act

questions.explanation: B and T cells each recognise one antigen shape, so the response targets one pathogen. Option B is wrong because the specific response acts against viruses and other pathogens too.

questions.prompt: A person recovers from chickenpox and does not catch it again when exposed years later. The best explanation is that:

options.C: phagocytes have learned the shape of the virus
options.D: memory cells recognise the virus and trigger a rapid response

questions.explanation: Memory cells made during the first infection quickly produce plasma cells and antibodies. Phagocytes are non-specific and do not form memory, so option C is wrong.

questions.prompt: Smoking damages cilia in the airways. Which outcome is most likely?

options.A: Mucus and trapped pathogens are not cleared well, so lung infections become more likely
options.B: The body makes more antibodies to replace the cilia

questions.explanation: Cilia sweep mucus and trapped pathogens out of the airways; without them, mucus builds up and infections are more likely. Antibodies cannot do the job of cilia, so option B is wrong.

questions.prompt: A student catches a cold in May and another cold in August. Which is the best explanation?

options.A: The student has no immune system
options.B: Antibodies only last a few days
options.C: The second cold was probably caused by a different virus with different antigens

questions.explanation: Many different viruses cause colds, and memory cells for one do not match the antigens of another. Option B is tempting, but memory cells can last a long time; the issue is a different antigen.

questions.prompt: In a second infection by the same pathogen, compared with the first infection, the antibody response is:

options.D: absent because the pathogen is recognised

questions.explanation: Memory cells allow plasma cells and antibodies to be made quickly and in greater numbers. Option D is wrong because recognition triggers a strong antibody response rather than no response.
